summary: Round 9. The two sentences round 8 blocked on are gone and AGENTS.md, code-structure.md, the backlog cell and io_seam_scan.py's PACKAGES comment are all TRUE at these bytes. But the same round that added javax.sql and javax.naming left scripts/check-io-seam.sh's own header saying TEN PACKAGES and enumerating ten -- the fourth document, and the one an author reads when the gate fails. That is the recurring class and it blocks. Everything else is a minor or a row: two measured false refusals (java.io.BufferedInputStream / java.io.EOFException, and a record accessor named nanoTime()), two measured package-half gaps (javax.xml.parsers, java.rmi) that the tree now openly admits are possible, and one stale denominator in the backlog cell. No object-store request is added or changed by this commit: the gate is a static text scan run at the pre-commit stage, so its cost scales with source files at commit time and with nothing at runtime.

findings.title: scripts/check-io-seam.sh's header says TEN packages and lists ten; the scanner it fronts bans TWELVE
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED at the staged bytes in a throwaway worktree. `python3 -c 'import io_seam_scan; print(len(io_seam_scan.PACKAGES))'` prints 12, and the list is java.nio.file, java.nio.channels, java.io, java.util.zip, java.net, javax.net, java.util.logging, java.sql, java.util.jar, java.util.prefs, javax.sql, javax.naming. scripts/check-io-seam.sh line 6 reads '# WARNING TEN PACKAGES ARE BANNED OUTRIGHT; THE CLOCK AND THE SUBPROCESS ARE NAMED BY CONSTRUCT.' and lines 7-10 enumerate exactly ten, omitting javax.sql and javax.naming -- the two added by the previous round, for the measured javax.sql.DataSource escape. AGENTS.md:153, docs/internal/standards/code-structure.md:20 and the M0.107 backlog cell all say TWELVE and all enumerate twelve correctly; check-io-seam.sh is the one document left behind. It is also the document an author reads FIRST, because it is the script named in the FAIL output and in .pre-commit-config.yaml. Consequence a reader suffers: the header's own next sentence says 'Each PACKAGE a reach can live in must be named', so a reader auditing the ban list against that instruction reads ten names, concludes javax.sql and javax.naming are unhandled, and either re-adds them (a no-op that looks like a fix) or re-derives the round-8 escape that is already closed. This is the identical class that blocked rounds 1 through 8 -- a claim about the list stated in one of four documents and falsified by the code beside it -- and it was introduced by the round whose whole subject was that list. FIX: line 6 'TWELVE PACKAGES', and add `javax.sql` and `javax.naming` to the enumeration on lines 7-10.

findings.title: Correct code the gate refuses: java.io.BufferedInputStream and java.io.EOFException
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED at the staged bytes. File written to ingest/src/main/java/binjava/ingest/P3.java, valid Java, staged, `./scripts/check-io-seam.sh --full` exit 1 with two FAILs: `java.io reaches the filesystem directly` at the `import java.io.BufferedInputStream;` line and at the `import java.io.EOFException;` line. The body was `InputStream buffered(InputStream in) { return new BufferedInputStream(in); }` plus a read loop throwing `new EOFException("truncated segment")`. Neither reaches anything: BufferedInputStream wraps a stream the caller handed in, and EOFException is an exception type in exactly the category ALLOWED already carves out three members of (IOException, UncheckedIOException, FileNotFoundException). The scanner's own comment at line 166-169 says the sibling names are 'listed ahead of need so the first use of `Flushable` is not a spurious refusal' -- but the two siblings a segment reader reaches for first, a buffering wrapper and an end-of-stream exception, are not among them. The backlog cell states the risk itself: 'a gate that refuses correct code is one an author edits rather than obeys'. NOT BLOCKING: the refusal is loud, names the package, and the documented workflow (add the entry with a sample that must be ACCEPTED) is available; no file in the tree is affected today. Adding entries here is a one-line change to ALLOWED plus one line in IoSeamGateTest's `accepted` map, and per review.md rule 11 it is legitimate to land this as a row instead.

findings.title: A record accessor named nanoTime() is refused, and the backlog cell's generalisation about receiver anchoring is false for two of the clock entries
findings.file: scripts/io_seam_scan.py:58-64; docs/internal/product/backlog.md M0.107 cell, final sentence
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED at the staged bytes: `record P4(long nanoTime, String key) { long age(long readAt) { return readAt - nanoTime(); } }` under ingest/src/main/java/binjava/ingest/ is refused, exit 1, 'nanoTime( reaches the real clock directly'. A producer-supplied timestamp carried on a record is ordinary business logic and sources no clock. The cause is correct and deliberate -- `currentTimeMillis(` and `nanoTime(` have no dot, so _shape's bare-call arm builds an unanchored regex on purpose, to catch the static-import form the comment at lines 59-62 says review measured escaping. What is not correct is the M0.107 cell's closing sentence: 'the clock entries anchor their receiver to a capitalised name, so a record accessor named `now()` reaches nothing and passes'. The conclusion about `now()` is true and I verified the anchoring in _shape's `literal.endswith('()')` arm; the premise stated of 'the clock entries' as a class is false for two of the nine, and the scanner's own comment says so ('No receiver to anchor, so the name alone must carry it'). A reader who trusts the cell concludes no accessor name can collide, which the nanoTime measurement falsifies. NOT BLOCKING: the sentence's payload is true, the overreach is in a subordinate clause, and the trade-off it describes (a static import must be caught without a receiver) is right. Either narrow the clause to 'the `.now()` and `.now(...)` entries' or drop it.

findings.title: Two reaches in the PACKAGE half whose packages are not listed: javax.xml.parsers and java.rmi
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED at the staged bytes, two files under ingest/src/main/java/binjava/ingest/, both staged, `./scripts/check-io-seam.sh --full` exit 0 ('ok 103 business-logic file(s) name none of the 28 banned constructs'). (a) `DocumentBuilderFactory.newInstance().newDocumentBuilder().parse(path)` -- javax.xml.parsers, and `parse(String)` opens the file or URL named by the argument. (b) `java.rmi.Naming.lookup(name)` -- opens a socket to a registry. Neither package is in PACKAGES and neither call shape is in BANNED. THIS IS A ROW, NOT A BLOCK, and deliberately so at these bytes: the round-8 fix makes every document say the package half is 'as complete as its list of packages' and the scanner comment at lines 108-114 says 'This list grows when a reader finds a package a reach lives in'. These two are exactly that -- a gap in a list the tree openly calls incomplete, which is a different thing from the false claim that blocked the previous eight rounds. Recording them so the next reader has the two names rather than the argument: add ('javax.xml.parsers', DISK) and ('java.rmi', SOCKET) with samples in IoSeamGateTest's `refused` map when someone is in this file anyway.

findings.title: The backlog cell says 'one class of forty'; the tree has 101 non-exempt business-logic files and the test javadoc says 'one class of a hundred'
findings.failure_scenario: MEASURED at the staged bytes: `git ls-files -- '*/src/main/java/binjava/*.java' | grep -vc '^binstore-backends/'` prints 101, and the gate's own success line on the clean tree prints '101 business-logic file(s)'. The M0.107 cell argues 'a one-off test here would cover one class of forty', while IoSeamGateTest's class javadoc makes the same argument as 'covers one class of a hundred'. The javadoc is right; the cell understates by 2.5x. NOT BLOCKING and NOT the recurring class: the denominator is not marked MEASURED, the argument it supports holds at either number, and the cell is prose about why the task was numbered M0 rather than a claim about what the code does. Worth one word if the cell is edited for R9-1 anyway; not worth a round of its own.
